newsitem.title: MEXICO: Sidek restructuring delay seen positive.
newsitem.headline: Sidek restructuring delay seen positive.

text.p: Analysts on Wednesday welcomed a reported agreement between Mexican steel conglomerate Sidek and its creditor banks to extend by five months the period in which it draws up a restructuring plan.
"If you're on death row, any stay of execution is good news," said Santiago Pique of Bear Stearns in New York.

He speculated that one of the purposes of the delay was to enable Sidek, and its tourism subsidiary Situr, to remain with salvageable businesses under a plan in which it has said it will retire $1 billion of debt by selling off a large chunk of its assets. The company owes some $2.1 billion.

On Wednesday, Reforma newspaper published an interview with new Sidek CEO Luis Rebollar in which he said the banks had agreed to extend until November 29 the period in which Sidek maintains a halt on its debt payments while it rethinks its restructuring plan.

It had originally said it would present the new plan on June 30. On Wednesday, its heavily-traded B shares were up 3 centavos to 1.55 pesos, while the A series was off 7.78 percent on wafer-thin volume.

Analysts said one of the reasons for the delay was the entry of Rebollar in June as head of the Guadalajara firm. He is said to be more attentive to foreign bond holders who were unhapppy with the original debt restructuring plan unveiled in April because they were left as the least senior creditors.
"There's a lot of sourness at the way things were handled in the past. Sidek is now concerned about it and they're finding a way to make it better," one foreign banker said.

For Martin Lara, analyst at Caspian Securities, permission to extend the suspension of debt payments for five months was good for stock holders, and he welcomed the fact that the restructuring plan was underway.

He also noted that the real estate market for selling off assets like hotels and marines owned by Situr was only barely starting to pick up. So far, he said, Sidek was only selling off its smallest units like factoring firm Kapital Haus.
